planting.note: Best planted in a hanging container or on a raised ledge so the trailing stems can cascade freely.

directions: Grow in a fast-draining cactus mix and set in bright light with some protection from the harshest midday sun. Allow the soil to dry completely between waterings, cutting back watering almost entirely in winter. Propagate easily from stem cuttings left to callus for several days before rooting. Feed sparingly with a low-nitrogen cactus fertilizer during the active summer growing season to encourage the tubular orange-red flowers.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America (cssainc.org)

planting.note: Site in a spot with reflected warmth, since this cactus resents cool, damp conditions.

directions: Plant in a gritty, mineral-heavy cactus soil that drains within seconds of watering. Provide full sun to develop the dense white woolly hair that covers the ribbed columnar stem, since low light produces sparse, thin covering. Water deeply but infrequently in summer and keep nearly dry through winter to prevent rot at the base. Because it is slow to reach flowering size, most gardeners grow it primarily as a striking architectural foliage specimen.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America (cssainc.org)

planting.note: Choose a permanent, well-drained bed, as this barrel cactus resents being moved once its taproot establishes.

directions: Grow in coarse, gritty soil with excellent drainage and plenty of direct sun to keep the barrel shape symmetrical and the amber spines dense. Water sparingly through the growing season and withhold water almost entirely once temperatures drop in fall. This species tolerates brief light frost better than many barrel cacti once mature, making it a good candidate for marginal desert climates. Established plants are traditionally tapped for their sweet sap, which is boiled down into a regional candy, but this is unnecessary for garden cultivation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America (cssainc.org)

planting.note: Stake young columnar stems loosely until roots anchor them, especially in windy sites.

directions: Plant in loose, fast-draining soil and situate in full sun for the sturdiest, most blue-green columnar growth. Water regularly through spring and summer, letting the soil dry between sessions, then reduce sharply in winter. Large night-blooming white flowers appear on mature stems in summer and last only a single night, so check plants at dusk if you want to see them open. This species is markedly more cold-tolerant than many South American columnar cacti, surviving brief dips near freezing once established.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America (cssainc.org)
Huntington Botanical Gardens cactus collection notes

planting.note: Allow generous overhead clearance, since this columnar species eventually grows tree-like and branches with age.

directions: Set in full sun and gritty, mineral soil with sharp drainage to replicate its native Argentine scrubland habitat. Water deeply but only occasionally in the warm season and keep essentially dry through winter dormancy. Growth is slow for the first several years while the plant builds a sturdy base, after which it can add height quickly and eventually branch into a tree-like form resembling its North American saguaro namesake. It is among the more frost-hardy tall columnar cacti, tolerating brief cold snaps that would damage related species.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America (cssainc.org)
